title: Cold Water, Full Nets
question: How does wind bring deep ocean water to the surface, and why does it matter for fish?
hook: Five patches of sea covering just 5% of the ocean supply about a quarter of the world's marine fish catch.
idea: When wind and the Coriolis effect move surface water apart, cool nutrient-rich deep water rises to replace it and feeds the base of the food chain.

beats.prompt: Put these steps of upwelling in order.
items: Wind blows across the sea surface
Surface water is moved at an angle to the wind
Deep, nutrient-rich water rises to replace it
Phytoplankton grow on the new nutrients
beats.explain: Wind moves the surface water sideways, deep water rises where it diverges, and the nutrients it brings feed phytoplankton.

beats.prompt: A steady wind blows across the sea south of the equator. Overall, which way does the surface water move?

choices.label: To the right of the wind
choices.feedback: That is the Northern Hemisphere rule; south of the equator the turn goes the other way.

choices.label: To the left of the wind
Straight along with the wind
choices.feedback: It feels natural, but the net movement ends up about 90 degrees from the wind.

choices.label: Directly against the wind
choices.feedback: Nothing pushes water back into the wind; it is turned sideways instead.

beats.explain: Coriolis forces and Ekman transport send the water a net 90 degrees from the wind, to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.

beats.prompt: Sort each description into the water it fits.
beats.explain: Upwelling lifts dense, cool, nutrient-rich water and swaps it for warmer, nutrient-poor surface water.

beats.prompt: Match each upwelling current to the coast it runs along.
beats.explain: These are among the five major coastal currents tied to upwelling, and all support major fisheries.
